name: Swiss editorial
philosophy: Make relationships legible through alignment, scale and ordering. The grid is a compositional instrument, not a reason to turn every item into a card.
influences: Contemporary interpretation of International Typographic Style: flush alignment, sans-serif hierarchy and disciplined asymmetry. This is practical art direction, not a sourced history of the movement.
characteristics: A small number of strong alignment lines
Unequal columns with a clear reading sequence
Display typography that carries the composition
typography: Use a robust grotesk with distinct figures and adequate language coverage. A system sans is an acceptable prototype. Contrast sizes before adding families. Set body at 1rem–1.125rem, line-height 1.5–1.65, measure 55–70ch. Large headlines may tighten tracking; don't apply that to body text.
color: Start with a paper/ink pair and one navigational accent. Accent may occupy a whole information band; it is not restricted to a single word. Test accent links on the actual background.
spacing: Use 4/8/12/20/32/48/80px roles; tighter caption-to-image spacing than project-to-project spacing. Whitespace expresses relationships, not luxury by default.
composition: Twelve desktop columns are a starting hypothesis: headline 8, context 4; project row 5/7. On mobile, use one reading column, retaining asymmetry through type and spacing rather than offscreen content.
imagery: Use contextual photographs or original diagrams whose crop explains the subject. Caption factual images. Repeated aspect ratios establish rhythm; one justified panoramic interruption can signal a new topic.
iconography: Sparse functional symbols; label unfamiliar actions. Optical alignment matters more than putting every mark in a decorative container.
components: Prefer ruled project lists, clear navigation and compact metadata. Distinguish headings from clickable project names. Buttons can be rectangular; click targets still need adequate area.
interaction: Project links navigate to real sections or pages. Filters should announce changed counts and retain the current selection. Preserve browser back behavior.
motion: Use quick state feedback or a single editorial transition. Scrolling should not be required to reveal essential text. A static layout should remain complete.
mobile: Collapse the layout in DOM reading order; do not use CSS order to conceal a confused source order. Permit long titles to wrap. Reduce display scale with clamp() while leaving the body readable.
accessibility: Grid position cannot be the sole indicator of grouping. Use headings, lists and landmarks; check focus across full-width links, zoom and text spacing overrides.
mistakes: Numbering unordered content as if it were a process
Tiny labels used to compensate for excessive headline size
Rigid columns that truncate translated titles
amateurish: Decorative rules everywhere, arbitrary offsets and exaggerated tracking without a coherent reading sequence.
exceptional: Different content has distinct weight while recurring elements land on shared edges. Crops and typography express the actual discipline of the client.
implementation: Use CSS grid with minmax(0, 1fr), a named content container and shared row borders. Try grid-template-columns: 5fr 7fr above 50rem; one column below. See the original editorial example.
libraries: Native Grid and fluid CSS usually suffice. No font or animation package is required; license any chosen webfont independently.
evaluation: Can a reader identify subject, author and primary next step in one scan?
Do project titles remain distinct from their metadata at 320px?
Does asymmetry reinforce the content rather than scramble reading order?
evidence: Original design recipe; source-linked engineering constraints. Not a validated causal model of visual quality.
